english: I'm here to get my Alien Registration Card issued
usage: 외국인등록증 발급받으러 왔어요
I came to get my ARC issued
Polite; said at the counter to state your purpose
외국인등록증 발급받으러 왔어
I came to get my ARC
반말, only if explaining to a friend, never to staff
외국인등록증 발급받으러 왔는데요
I'm here to get my ARC, and…
Softer -는데요 ending that invites the clerk to guide you
외국인등록 신청하러 왔어요
I came to apply for foreigner registration
Focus on the application act (신청) rather than the card object
examples: 외국인등록증 발급받으러 왔어요.
I'm here to get my ARC issued.
The single opening line that tells staff exactly why you came; hold up your passport as you say it
A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 외국인등록증 발급받으러 왔는데요, 어디로 가면 돼요?
A: How can I help you? / B: I'm here to get my ARC — where should I go?
A/B counter exchange: 어떻게 오셨어요 is the standard 'how can I help' from staff; chain -는데요 to keep the door open for guidance
처음이라 외국인등록증 발급받으러 왔는데 뭐부터 해야 돼요?
It's my first time getting my ARC — what do I do first?
처음이라 ('since it's my first time') signals you need a full walk-through; staff will slow down and guide you step by step
nuance: 외국인등록증 발급받으러 왔어요 is the core opening line at 출입국 (Immigration) or a service center: 외국인등록증 ('Alien Registration Card', mandatory for every foreigner staying over 90 days) + 발급받다 ('to be issued / receive issuance') + -으러 왔어요 ('came in order to'). In everyday speech both applicants and staff routinely shorten it to 등록증. Register is plain 존댓말 (-어요), exactly right for a government counter — not stiff 합쇼체, not casual 반말. The grammar trap for English speakers is the -으러 ending: it attaches to a verb stem to mean 'in order to do', so it must ride on 받으러 (the verb), NOT on the noun — 외국인등록증으로 왔어요 means 'I came BY MEANS OF the ARC', confusing -으러 ('in order to') with -으로 ('by/with'). The near-synonym 외국인등록 신청하러 왔어요 ('I came to APPLY for registration') differs: use 신청하러 when starting paperwork; 발급받으러 when the focus is collecting the physical card. The 직역 pitfall: translating 'I want to register' as 등록하고 싶어요 sounds like a vague wish; at a counter state purpose with -으러 왔어요. Also note 발급받다 (you receive) vs 발급하다 (the office issues) — the applicant always 발급받다.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: 외국인등록증(ARC) + 발급받(receive issuance of) + -으러 왔어요(came in order to). The real function: a single counter-opening statement that tells staff your purpose instantly so they can route you correctly. In speech 외국인등록증 is often shortened to 등록증 by both sides.

Used exclusively at the 출입국 counter or a government service center. Register is plain 존댓말 (-어요) — the everyday polite level, not the stiff 합쇼체 (too formal) and never 반말 (too casual with a stranger official). You say this while presenting your passport, typically within the first five seconds of approaching the window.

외국인등록 신청하러 왔어요 ('came to APPLY') vs 발급받으러 왔어요 ('came to receive the card'). Use 신청하러 on your first visit when paperwork has not yet been lodged; use 발급받으러 when you are returning to collect the card. Also note 발급받다 (applicant) vs 발급하다 (office issues) — mixing these up sounds like you work there.

-으러 왔어요 → -으러 왔는데요 (softer, invites guidance) → -으려고 하는데요 (slightly more tentative, 'I'm trying to…'). In short speech at a busy counter just 등록증 발급받으러요 ('here for the ARC') is understood. Never drop the -으러 and say 등록증 왔어요 — that sounds like 'the card came'.

Two traps: (1) confusing -으러 ('in order to', purposive) with -으로 ('by means of') — 외국인등록증으로 왔어요 means 'I came by/with the ARC' (bizarre). (2) Translating 'I want to register' as 등록하고 싶어요 — at a service counter you state your purpose with -으러 왔어요, not a desire with -고 싶어요.

mistakes: Saying 외국인등록증으로 왔어요 to mean 'I came for my ARC'.
-으로 means 'by means of', so this reads 'I came using the ARC'. The 'in order to' ending attaches to the verb: 발급받으러 왔어요.
Using 발급했어요 about yourself.
발급하다 is what the OFFICE does (issues the card). The applicant RECEIVES it, so say 발급받으러 왔어요 / 발급받았어요, not 발급했어요.
Translating 'I want to register' as 등록하고 싶어요 at the counter.
-고 싶어요 sounds like a personal wish. State your purpose for being there: 외국인등록 하러 왔어요 or 발급받으러 왔어요.

english: I'd like to extend my stay
usage: 체류 기간 연장하고 싶어요
I'd like to extend my period of stay
Polite; the standard way to state the visit's purpose
체류 기간 연장하려고 왔어요
I came to extend my stay
States it as the reason you're physically here
체류 연장하러 왔는데요
I'm here to extend my stay, and…
Short everyday form with the soft -는데요 lead-in
비자 연장하고 싶어요
I'd like to extend my visa
Everyday phrasing — many say 비자 연장 for 체류 연장
examples: 체류 기간 연장하고 싶어요.
I'd like to extend my period of stay.
A clear one-line purpose statement at the counter; follow immediately with 어떻게 해야 돼요? if you need guidance
A: 어떻게 도와드릴까요? / B: 다음 달에 비자 끝나서 체류 기간 연장하려고 왔어요.
A: How can I help you? / B: My status ends next month, so I came to extend my stay.
A/B exchange: give the reason with -아서 ('because') before the purpose; 어떻게 도와드릴까요 is the formal staff opener
체류 연장하려면 어떤 서류가 필요해요?
What documents do I need to extend my stay?
-려면 ('if I want to') asks what's required; use after the staff confirms which desk handles it
nuance: 체류 기간 연장 is the official term for extending your authorized stay: 체류 ('staying/residence', 滯留) + 기간 ('period') + 연장 ('extension', 延長). On forms and signs you'll see 체류기간 연장허가 ('permission to extend period of stay'), so this phrase matches the bureaucracy exactly. In everyday speech many foreigners and even staff say 비자 연장 ('visa extension'), which is understood — but technically you extend your 체류 기간 (the authorized stay tied to your status), while the 비자 (the entry sticker) is a different thing; for officials, 체류 기간 연장 is precise. The key grammar contrast: use -하고 싶어요 ('I'd like to') to state the goal politely, or -하러/하려고 왔어요 ('I came in order to') to frame it as the reason you're there — both are natural and officials respond to either. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is confusing 연장 (extension, adding time) with 갱신 (renewal, re-issuing an expiring document): saying 체류 기간 갱신 confuses the clerk about which service you need. Register is plain 존댓말. Never say 체류만 연장 without 기간 — dropping both sounds truncated; the accepted short form is 체류 연장 (not 체류만).

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: 체류(stay/residence) + 기간(period) + 연장(extension) + 하고 싶어요(I'd like to do). The real function: formally stating at the counter that you want to add more authorized time to your stay, which triggers the correct service queue and document checklist.

Said at the 출입국 window when your current visa status or D-period is approaching expiry (usually applied 2–3 months before). Register is plain 존댓말; using 합쇼체 (합니다 form) is acceptable but sounds stiff from a foreigner. Using 반말 with staff is always wrong. You must apply before expiry — staff may note the deadline immediately.

비자 연장 vs 체류 기간 연장: both are heard, but 비자 연장 is imprecise — the visa sticker and the stay period are legally different objects. With an official always say 체류 기간 연장. Also: 연장 (adding time to an existing status) vs 갱신 (re-issuing an expiring document like an ARC card) — picking the wrong one sends you to the wrong window.

-하고 싶어요 (I'd like to) → -하러 왔어요 (I came to) → -하려고 왔어요 (I came intending to) — all natural. Short form: 체류 연장하러요 at a busy counter. The polite question form 체류 기간 연장 가능한가요? ('Is extension possible?') works if you're unsure whether you qualify.

연장 vs 갱신 confusion is the top error: learners reach for 갱신 ('renewal') because English says 'renew a visa', but 갱신 in Korean is for re-issuing an expiring document, not adding stay time. Also 체류를 늘리고 싶어요 ('I want to increase my stay') — 늘리다 is too physical/informal; the bureaucratic verb is 연장하다.

mistakes: Confusing 연장 (extension) with 갱신 (renewal).
연장 adds time to your stay; 갱신 re-issues an expiring document. To stay longer, say 체류 기간 연장; to replace an expiring ARC, say 갱신.
Saying 체류를 늘리고 싶어요.
늘리다 ('to increase/lengthen') is too literal/physical here. The fixed bureaucratic verb is 연장하다: 체류 기간 연장하고 싶어요.
Treating 비자 and 체류 기간 as identical to an official.
Casually 비자 연장 is fine, but precisely you extend 체류 기간 (your stay). For accuracy with staff, say 체류 기간 연장.

english: What type of visa is it?
usage: 비자 종류가 뭐예요?
What's the visa type?
Polite-neutral; asking which visa category applies
무슨 비자예요?
What visa is it?
Everyday, slightly more casual phrasing
제 비자가 무슨 종류예요?
What type is my visa?
Asking specifically about your own visa status
비자 종류가 어떻게 되세요?
May I ask your visa type?
Honorific 어떻게 되세요 — what STAFF say to you
examples: 제 비자 종류가 뭐예요?
What type is my visa?
Asking the clerk to confirm your category; hold out your ARC or passport so they can check
A: 비자 종류가 어떻게 되세요? / B: E-7이요.
A: May I ask your visa type? / B: It's E-7.
A/B counter exchange showing the register split: staff use honorific 어떻게 되세요; you answer plainly with just the code
이 일 하려면 비자 종류가 뭐예요? 바꿔야 돼요?
What visa type do I need for this job — do I have to change it?
Link to 바꿔야 돼요 ('do I have to change it?') to ask about status change; 이 일 하려면 = 'if I want to do this job'
nuance: 비자 종류가 뭐예요? is 비자 ('visa') + 종류 ('type/kind', 種類) + 가 뭐예요 ('what is'), used to ask or confirm which visa category is in play. Korea has alphanumeric visa codes (D-2 student, E-2 English teacher, E-7 skilled worker, F-6 marriage, etc.) and every counter service depends on which code you hold, so confirming 종류 is often the first thing a clerk does. The crucial register split: a clerk asks YOU honorifically, 비자 종류가 어떻게 되세요? — 어떻게 되세요 is the respectful 'how is it / may I ask', aimed at the customer — and you answer plainly with the code, 'E-7이요'. If YOU ask, the neutral 비자 종류가 뭐예요? or casual 무슨 비자예요? is right; never bounce 어떻게 되세요 back at yourself. The formal document term is 체류자격 ('status of stay'), what you see on official papers — if you want to sound bureaucratically precise, 체류자격이 어떻게 되세요? is what appears on intake forms. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'what is my visa status' as 제 비자 상태가 뭐예요? — in Korean 상태 ('condition/state') means 'is it valid/okay?', not 'which category'; for the category, say 종류 or 체류자격. Particle note: it's 종류'가' 뭐예요 (subject particle), not 종류'를'.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: 비자(visa) + 종류가(type — subject) + 뭐예요(what is). The real function: confirming the alphanumeric status code that determines which services, extensions, and work rights apply to you. Every immigration service branches by 종류, so naming it correctly is step one.

Used at the 출입국 counter when the clerk needs to verify your category before processing, or when you need to confirm which code you hold before asking about a service. The register split is important: staff ask you with honorific 어떻게 되세요; you ask the clerk with plain 뭐예요. Using honorifics about your own visa (제 비자가 어떻게 되세요?) is a self-honorification error.

비자 종류 (informal, spoken) vs 체류자격 (formal, on documents): both mean visa category. Using 체류자격 with a clerk sounds polished and matches the form they're filling out. Separately, 비자 상태 ('visa condition/status') is asking whether your visa is valid or problematic — not which type it is — so it is a different question entirely.

뭐예요? (plain) → 어떻게 되세요? (honorific, staff → you) → 어떻게 되나요? (slightly more formal self-ask). Short answers: 'E-7이요' / 'D-2예요' / 'F-6이에요' — just the code plus the copula. Never answer 저도 몰라요 ('I don't know') to staff; look it up on your card first.

Saying 비자 상태가 뭐예요 when you mean 'which category' — 상태 means condition/health of the visa, not its type. Also: using 종류'를' 뭐예요 — 를 marks an object and is ungrammatical here; the subject particle 가 is correct. And echoing the honorific back onto yourself: 제 비자 종류가 어떻게 되세요 — that honorifies yourself, which is wrong.

mistakes: Answering a clerk's 어떻게 되세요? with 어떻게 돼요 about yourself.
어떻게 되세요 is honorific, aimed AT you. You answer plainly: just state the code, 'F-6이요', not by re-asking 어떻게 돼요.
Saying 비자 상태가 뭐예요 to mean 'which category'.
상태 ('state/condition') sounds like asking if it's valid. For the category, say 비자 종류가 뭐예요 or the formal 체류자격.
Using 를 instead of 가: 비자 종류를 뭐예요.
'What is X' takes the subject particle: 비자 종류가 뭐예요. 를 marks an object and is ungrammatical with 뭐예요.

english: How do I fill out the application form?
usage: 신청서 어떻게 작성해요?
How do I fill out the application form?
Polite; asking staff to guide you through the form
신청서 어떻게 써요?
How do I write the application?
Everyday 쓰다 instead of formal 작성하다
이거 어떻게 작성하는지 알려 주세요
Please show me how to fill this out
-는지 알려 주세요 asks them to teach you the how
여기 뭐 적어요?
What do I write here?
Pointing at one blank field on the form
examples: 이 신청서 어떻게 작성해요?
How do I fill out this application form?
Hold up the blank form to staff; this single line prompts them to either walk you through it or direct you to a help desk
A: 여기 뭐 적어요? / B: 거기는 현재 주소 적으시면 돼요.
A: What do I write here? / B: Write your current address there.
A/B exchange pointing at a specific field; 거기는 ('there') + 적으시면 돼요 is the natural staff reply
이 칸은 뭘 적는지 몰라서요, 어떻게 작성해요?
I don't know what goes in this box — how do I fill it in?
칸 ('box/field') + -는지 몰라서 ('because I don't know what goes in') explains your confusion; the soft trailing 몰라서요 is very natural spoken Korean
nuance: 신청서 어떻게 작성해요? is 신청서 ('application form', 申請書) + 어떻게 ('how') + 작성하다 ('to fill out / draw up', 作成), the line that gets a clerk to walk you through the paperwork. 작성하다 is the proper, slightly formal verb for completing a form or official document; in casual speech 쓰다 ('write') or 적다 ('jot/note') are used and 어떻게 써요? is perfectly natural and a bit warmer. The dividing line between these verbs: 작성하다 is for filling out a whole document (a form, an application, a report), while 적다/쓰다 fit a single field — so 'how do I fill out the form' is 작성, but 'what do I write in this box' is 여기 뭐 적어요?. The near-synonym 기입하다 ('to enter/inscribe') shows up on official written instructions but sounds bookish aloud; stick with 작성/적다 when speaking. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'fill out' as 채우다 ('to fill a container') — 신청서를 채워요 sounds like physically stuffing the form, not completing it; the right verb is 작성하다. Particle note: object marker can be dropped in natural speech (신청서 작성해요 rather than 신청서를 작성해요). Register is plain 존댓말. A very common follow-up is 영어로 작성해도 돼요? ('can I fill this out in English?') — asking permission to use English on the form.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: 신청서(application form) + 어떻게(how) + 작성해요(do I fill out). The real function: prompting a clerk to walk you through unfamiliar paperwork rather than attempting to guess at fields you don't understand, which prevents costly mistakes.

Said at the counter after receiving a blank form, or at a service desk when you're confused by a specific field. Register is plain 존댓말. You can soften it with 죄송한데요 ('sorry, but') or 잘 모르겠어서요 ('because I'm not sure') as a lead-in. This is appropriate for any clerk or helper — not too formal, not too casual.

작성하다 (whole-form, official) vs 쓰다/적다 (individual field, everyday). If you point at a single blank: 여기 뭐 적어요? If you want them to show you the whole form: 신청서 어떻게 작성해요? The formal 기입하다 appears in printed instructions but is rarely spoken aloud — use 작성 or 적다 in conversation.

작성해요? (neutral) → 작성하면 돼요? (permission-seeking, 'is it okay to fill out like this?') → 작성하는지 알려 주세요 (asking them to show you how). Shorter: 이거 어떻게 써요? is the fastest casual version. Follow-up: 영어로 작성해도 돼요? ('may I write in English?') — 도 돼요 checks permission.

채우다 ('to fill a container') as a translation of 'fill out' — 신청서를 채워요 sounds like stuffing the form physically. The right verb is 작성하다 for the whole form or 적다 for a field. Also 기입하다 sounds bureaucratic in speech; spoken Korean prefers 작성/적다.

mistakes: Saying 신청서를 채워요 for 'fill out the form'.
채우다 means filling a container (a cup, a tank). Completing a form uses 작성하다: 신청서 어떻게 작성해요?
Using 작성하다 for one tiny field.
작성 is for a whole document. For a single box ask 여기 뭐 적어요? or 뭐 써요? — 적다/쓰다 fit individual fields better.
Confusing 신청서 (application form) with 신청 (the act of applying).
신청서 is the paper; 신청 is applying. 'How do I fill out the FORM' needs 신청서: 신청서 어떻게 작성해요?

usage: 어디에서 접수해요?
Where do I submit it?
Polite; asking where to hand in your paperwork
어디에서 접수하면 돼요?
Where should I submit it?
-면 돼요 ('where is fine to') sounds a touch softer
접수 어디서 해요?
Where's the intake?
Casual word order, common in quick speech
이거 여기서 접수돼요?
Can this be submitted here?
접수되다 (passive) checks if this counter takes it
examples: 이거 어디에서 접수해요?
Where do I submit this?
Holding your documents, asking which counter takes them; the most common first question after filling out a form
A: 서류 다 썼는데 어디에서 접수하면 돼요? / B: 저쪽 2번 창구로 가세요.
A: I've finished the forms — where do I submit them? / B: Please go to window 2 over there.
A/B exchange: 다 썼는데 ('I've finished and…') leads into the where-question; staff reply with 창구 ('window/counter') number
여기서 접수하고 번호표 뽑으면 돼요?
Do I submit here and then take a number ticket?
Linking 접수 with 번호표 뽑다 ('take a queue ticket') — common two-step process at bigger offices; -면 돼요 asks for confirmation
nuance: 어디에서 접수해요? is 어디에서 ('at where') + 접수하다 ('to submit / receive intake', 接受). 접수 is the bureaucratic word for the official intake of documents — handing in your application so it's logged and processed. It cuts both ways: as the applicant you 접수하다 (submit), and the office 접수받다 (receives/accepts) your case; the counter is the 접수처 or 접수 창구. The subtle point English speakers miss is that 접수 is NOT just 'hand over a paper' — it means the case is formally entered into the system, complete with a receipt slip (접수증), so 'I submitted and got a receipt number' is all captured by 접수. The near-synonym 제출하다 ('to submit/turn in', 提出) overlaps but leans toward handing over a specific document (a report, a certificate in an academic setting), while 접수 emphasizes the office accepting and registering your case — at immigration, 접수 is the word on every sign and ticket. The English-speaker pitfall is always translating 'submit' as 제출, then being baffled by 접수 on every sign; learn 접수 as the front-desk intake verb. Particle trap: location of an action takes -에서, NOT -에 (which marks a static spot or destination) — 어디에 접수해요 sounds slightly off. The passive 접수되다 ('to be accepted') is handy: 이거 접수돼요? ('will this be accepted here?').

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: 어디에서(where, at) + 접수해요(do the intake/submit). The real function: finding the correct window or counter to officially lodge your application so it enters the processing system — not just handing paper to any person, but reaching the designated 접수 point.

Said after completing your forms, when you're not sure which window is the intake point. Polite 존댓말 is perfect. You can add 이거 ('this') — 이거 어디에서 접수해요? — while holding up your packet to make the question concrete. Never use 반말 with staff even if they look young.

접수하다 (lodge a case into the system, government/hospital/office) vs 제출하다 (hand over a document, e.g., to a professor or employer). At immigration, 접수 appears on every sign; saying 제출하다 is understood but marks you as treating it like a school assignment rather than a bureaucratic intake. The passive 접수되다 ('to be received/logged') is useful to check eligibility: 이거 접수돼요?

어디에서 접수해요? → 어디에서 접수하면 돼요? (softer, permission-seeking) → 접수 어디서 해요? (fastest spoken form). Also: 이거 여기서 접수돼요? uses the passive to ask 'is this the right place for intake?'. Follow-up: 접수하고 나면 번호표 뽑아요? ('after intake do I take a number?').

Two traps: (1) always translating 'submit' as 제출, then not recognizing 접수 on signs — learn 접수 as the government intake verb. (2) Using -에 instead of -에서: 어디에 접수해요 — action location takes -에서; 어디에 sounds like asking where the counter IS (destination/static) rather than where the action happens.

mistakes: Using -에 instead of -에서 for the action: 어디에 접수해요.
An action's location takes -에서: 어디에서 접수해요? -에 marks a destination/static spot, which sounds off with the verb 접수하다.
Assuming 접수 just means handing over one paper.
접수 is the office formally receiving and logging your case. It covers submitting, getting a number, and being entered into the system — broader than 제출.
Mixing up 접수 (intake) and 영수증 (receipt).
접수 is submitting/intake; 영수증 is a payment receipt. After 접수 you may get a 접수증 (acknowledgment slip), not an 영수증. Keep them separate.

usage: 방문 예약하고 왔어요
I booked a visit and came
Polite; telling staff you have an online appointment
예약했는데요, 어디로 가요?
I have a reservation — where do I go?
Soft -는데요 lead-in then asks the way
예약 안 하고 왔는데 접수돼요?
I came without a reservation — can I still be seen?
Checks walk-in acceptance when you have no booking
예약 어떻게 해요?
How do I make a reservation?
Asking how to book if you haven't yet
examples: 오늘 2시로 방문 예약하고 왔어요.
I booked a 2 o'clock visit for today.
Give the time slot with -로 ('for') to confirm your booking; adds precision that helps staff find your name quickly
A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 하이코리아에서 예약했는데요, 여기 맞아요?
A: How can I help you? / B: I booked on HiKorea — is this the right place?
A/B exchange: mentioning the booking platform (HiKorea, the official site) helps staff pull up your reservation; 여기 맞아요 checks you're at the correct counter
예약 안 하면 오래 기다려요? 예약하고 오는 게 나아요?
Is the wait long without a reservation? Is it better to book first?
Compares walk-in vs booking with -는 게 나아요 ('is better'); a practical question if you're still deciding whether to make an appointment
nuance: 방문 예약하고 왔어요 is 방문 ('visit', 訪問) + 예약하다 ('to reserve/book', 豫約) + -하고 왔어요 ('did it and came'), the line that tells staff you hold an online appointment — essential because Korean immigration offices (출입국) now largely run on mandatory reservations through 하이코리아 (HiKorea), and walking in without one often means being turned away or a very long wait. The -하고 왔어요 structure ('I did X and came') is the natural way to report a completed precondition: you booked, then showed up. The key vocabulary pitfall is 예약 vs 약속: 예약 is a booked slot (restaurant, hospital, government office — an institution holds the spot), while 약속 is a personal agreement to meet someone — saying 약속하고 왔어요 would mean 'I made a personal promise and came', baffling a clerk. This 예약 vs 약속 mix-up is a classic English-speaker trap because English 'appointment' covers both. The 직역 pitfall: 'I have a reservation' rendered as 예약을 가지고 있어요 ('I possess a reservation') is unnatural — Korean says 예약했어요 ('I reserved') or 예약하고 왔어요. Note the contrast 예약 (booking ahead to secure a slot) vs 접수 (intake on arrival once you're there) — two different steps. Register is plain 존댓말. Particle: 2시'로' 예약 ('booked FOR 2 o'clock') uses -로 to mark the chosen time slot.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: 방문(visit) + 예약하고(having reserved) + 왔어요(came). The real meaning: I secured an appointment slot in advance and am now here to check in — as opposed to walking in and hoping for the best. The -하고 왔어요 construction packages a completed precondition with the current arrival.

Said the moment you approach the reception desk at 출입국. Most major offices require 하이코리아 (HiKorea) reservations; saying 방문 예약하고 왔어요 immediately shows you have a slot and prompts the clerk to search for your booking rather than send you to the walk-in queue. Register plain 존댓말. If the clerk can't find your booking, give the confirmation number (예약 번호).

예약 (institutional booking for a slot) vs 약속 (personal promise/meeting). 약속하고 왔어요 sounds like you made a personal promise to someone — deeply odd at a government counter. Also: 예약 (booking ahead) vs 접수 (intake on arrival) — two sequential steps you do on the same visit. 예약 안 하고 왔는데 접수돼요? ('I came without a booking — can I still submit?') is the useful no-reservation fallback.

방문 예약하고 왔어요 → 예약했어요 (shorter, 'I have a reservation') → 예약했는데요, 어디로 가요? (adds soft -는데요 and direction question). Giving the slot: 오늘 오전 10시로 예약했어요. If unsure of the counter: 예약했는데 담당 창구가 어디예요? ('I have a booking — which window handles it?').

예약 vs 약속 confusion caused by the English word 'appointment': 약속하고 왔어요 sounds bizarre at a counter. Also 예약을 가지고 있어요 ('I have/possess a reservation') is unnatural — say 예약했어요 ('I reserved'). Korean doesn't 'possess' a reservation.

mistakes: Saying 약속하고 왔어요 to mean 'I have an appointment'.
약속 is a personal promise/meeting. A booked office slot is 예약: 방문 예약하고 왔어요 / 예약했어요.
Over-literal 예약을 가지고 있어요 ('I have a reservation').
Korean doesn't 'possess' a reservation. Say 예약했어요 ('I reserved') or 예약하고 왔어요 ('I booked and came').
Confusing 예약 (book ahead) with 접수 (intake on arrival).
예약 secures a future slot; 접수 is submitting your case once you're there. Booking the visit is 예약, handing in papers is 접수.

english: Take a number ticket and wait
usage: 번호표 뽑고 기다리시면 돼요
Take a number and please wait
Honorific -시면 돼요 — what STAFF say to you
번호표 뽑으세요
Please take a number ticket
Short honorific command staff give
번호표 어디서 뽑아요?
Where do I take a number?
What YOU ask when you can't find the machine
번호표 뽑아야 돼요?
Do I need to take a number?
Checking whether a ticket is required first
examples: 저기 기계에서 번호표 뽑고 기다리시면 돼요.
Take a number from that machine and please wait.
기계 ('machine') points you to the ticket dispenser; -시면 돼요 is the honorific permission form staff use when directing customers
A: 번호표 뽑았는데 얼마나 기다려요? / B: 한 30분 정도요.
A: I took a number — how long is the wait? / B: About 30 minutes or so.
A/B exchange: 뽑았는데 ('I took it and…') naturally leads to a wait-time question; staff give an approximate answer with 정도
번호표 어디서 뽑아요? 안 보여서요.
Where do I take a number? I can't find it.
안 보여서요 ('because I can't see it') softens the ask with a reason; very natural spoken trailing sentence
nuance: 번호표 뽑고 기다리시면 돼요 is what the staff or a sign tells YOU: 번호표 ('number ticket', 番號票) + 뽑다 ('to pull/draw out', i.e. take from a dispenser) + 기다리다 ('wait') + -시면 돼요 (honorific 'you may / it's fine if you'). The verb for taking a queue ticket is specifically 뽑다 ('pull out'), the same verb as drawing a card or pulling a weed — Korean conceives of yanking the slip from the machine. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'take a ticket' as 가지다/가져가다 ('possess/carry'), giving 번호표 가져가세요, which sounds like 'take the ticket away with you'; the idiomatic verb is 뽑다. Register is the big lesson here: -시면 돼요 carries the honorific -시- because staff are politely addressing YOU the customer — when YOU talk about your own action, you drop -시-: 번호표 뽑고 기다릴게요 ('I'll take a number and wait'), never 뽑으시고 about your own action. The near-contrast: 줄 서다 ('to line up/stand in a queue') describes some offices that use physical lines instead of tickets — so 줄 서세요 ('please line up') and 번호표 뽑으세요 ('take a number') describe two different systems; don't stand in a line if the place uses 번호표 and vice versa. Plain version you'd use: 번호표 뽑아야 돼요? to check if a ticket is needed before approaching a random counter.

structuredNuance.t: What the staff or a sign tells YOU: 번호표(number ticket) + 뽑고(pull out and) + 기다리시면 돼요(it's fine if you wait). The key verb is 뽑다 ('pull out/draw'), which applies to any slip extracted from a machine, a card from a deck, or a weed from soil — in all cases the physical yanking action is the conceptual core.

Staff say this to direct you at the entrance of any busy government or hospital counter. The honorific -시면 돼요 is staff → customer; you never use -시면 돼요 about your own action. When you respond or describe yourself: 뽑고 기다릴게요 (drop -시-). If you haven't found the machine yet: 번호표 어디서 뽑아요?

번호표 뽑다 (take a ticket from a dispenser — the ticket-machine system) vs 줄 서다 (stand in a physical line). These are mutually exclusive systems; mixing them up wastes time. Some smaller offices use neither and just call you in order — in that case staff say 바로 오세요 ('come right up').

번호표 뽑고 기다리시면 돼요 (full staff instruction) → 번호표 뽑으세요 (shorter command) → 번호표 뽑아야 돼요? (your check: 'do I need to?') → 번호표 어디서 뽑아요? (your question: 'where?'). After taking a ticket: 몇 번까지 했어요? ('what number are they on?') checks how far the queue has moved.

번호표 가져가세요 ('take the ticket away') sounds like you want to pocket the slip permanently. The natural verb is 뽑다 ('pull/draw'). Also: self-applying the honorific from staff's sentence — saying 뽑으시고 기다릴게요 about your own action puts -시- on yourself, which is a self-honorification error.

mistakes: Saying 번호표 가져가세요 for 'take a number'.
가져가다 means 'carry it away'. Drawing a ticket from the dispenser is 뽑다: 번호표 뽑으세요 / 번호표 뽑고 기다리세요.
Echoing the honorific onto yourself: 저 번호표 뽑으시고 기다릴게요.
-시- honors the listener, not you. About your own action drop it: 번호표 뽑고 기다릴게요.
Confusing 번호표 (queue ticket) with 표 (a ticket like a movie/train ticket).
번호표 is specifically the numbered queue slip. A bare 표 could mean any ticket; for the waiting system say the full 번호표.

usage: 여기 서명하면 돼요?
Do I sign here?
Polite; confirming where to put your signature
여기 사인하면 돼요?
Do I sign here?
사인 (loanword 'sign') — very common in speech
어디에 서명해요?
Where do I sign?
Open question when no spot is indicated
서명만 하면 돼요?
Do I just need to sign?
만 ('only') checks if signing is all that's left
examples: 여기 서명하면 돼요?
Do I sign here?
Point at the signature line while asking; -면 돼요 is the 'is it okay if I…' confirmation pattern — far more natural than 서명해야 돼요 at this moment
A: 이름 쓰고 여기 서명하면 돼요? / B: 네, 도장이나 서명 둘 다 괜찮아요.
A: Do I write my name and sign here? / B: Yes, either a seal or signature is fine.
A/B exchange: the staff reply introduces 도장 (seal) as an alternative — a crucial piece of cultural knowledge for any foreigner
도장 없는데 서명해도 돼요?
I don't have a seal — can I sign instead?
도장 ('seal/stamp') vs 서명: Korean offices traditionally use seals; this question pre-empts the staff asking for your 도장 — know this before you go
nuance: 여기 서명하면 돼요? is 여기 ('here') + 서명하다 ('to sign', 署名) + -면 돼요? ('is it okay if I…?'), the line for confirming where your signature goes. Two words mean 'sign': the formal/native-feeling 서명 (what appears on official documents) and the loanword 사인 (from English 'sign', casual and very common in speech) — but beware that 사인 also means 'autograph (of a celebrity)', so in a formal sentence 서명 reads more cleanly. The bigger cultural point is 도장/인감 ('seal, name stamp'): Korea traditionally uses a carved name seal for official acts, so a clerk may ask 도장 있으세요? ('do you have a seal?'), and you can answer 도장 없는데 서명해도 돼요? ('I don't have a seal — may I sign instead?'). Knowing this saves a confusing moment. The -면 돼요? structure is the key polite confirm pattern meaning 'is it fine if I do [this]?'; learners often over-translate 'should I sign here' as 서명해야 돼요? ('must I sign?'), which asks about obligation rather than confirming the spot — for 'is THIS where I sign', use 여기 서명하면 돼요?. Register is plain 존댓말. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming a handwritten signature is always expected — the real concern is learning the word 도장 and having the vocabulary to ask for the signature alternative.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: 여기(here) + 서명하면(if I sign) + 돼요(is it okay). The real function: confirming the exact spot AND the permitted form (signature vs seal). The -면 돼요 frame means 'is it fine if I do this?' — it's a confirmation check, not an obligation question.

Used while the clerk is processing your application and points to a line, or when you spot a 서명 field and want to confirm. Register plain 존댓말. Cultural note: many Korean official documents have a 인감/도장 ('seal') field alongside or instead of a signature line — foreigners are generally allowed to substitute a handwritten signature, but you must ask explicitly with 서명해도 돼요?

서명 (written signature, formal, on documents) vs 사인 (loanword, casual, also means celebrity autograph) vs 도장 (carved name seal, traditional official Korean alternative). In a legal or bureaucratic context, 서명 is cleaner; 사인 is understood but sounds informal. The question 도장 없는데 서명해도 돼요? covers the most common scenario foreigners face.

여기 서명하면 돼요? (confirm spot + permission) → 어디에 서명해요? (open: where to sign at all) → 서명만 하면 돼요? (is signing the only thing left?). Combining: 이름 쓰고 여기 서명하면 돼요? ('write name and sign here?'). Staff may say: 여기 서명해 주세요 or 도장 찍어 주세요 ('please stamp here').

두 가지 함정: (1) 서명해야 돼요? vs 서명하면 돼요? — 해야 돼요 asks 'must I?' (obligation); 하면 돼요 asks 'is it okay if I?' (confirmation of spot). For confirming the location, use 하면 돼요. (2) Not knowing 도장 — many Korean forms still expect a seal, not a signature. Learn 도장 없는데 서명해도 돼요? as a ready-made fallback.

mistakes: Saying 서명해야 돼요? when you mean 'is this where I sign?'.
-해야 돼요 asks about obligation ('must I sign?'). To confirm the spot, use -하면 돼요: 여기 서명하면 돼요?
Not knowing 도장 and insisting only on a signature.
Korean offices often expect a 도장 (name seal). If asked 도장 있으세요?, you can say 도장 없는데 서명해도 돼요? to offer a signature instead.
Using 사인 in a strictly formal document context.
사인 is casual and also means 'autograph'. On official paperwork the cleaner word is 서명: 여기 서명하면 돼요?

english: Do you need a copy of my passport?
usage: 여권 사본 필요해요?
Do you need a passport copy?
Polite; asking if a photocopy is required
여권 사본 가져왔어요
I brought a passport copy
Stating you already have one ready
여권 원본도 필요해요?
Do you need the original too?
원본 ('original') vs 사본, a key document pair
사본 어디서 떼요?
Where can I make a copy?
떼다 ('to issue/make a copy'), where to get one
examples: 여권 사본 필요해요?
Do you need a copy of my passport?
Ask proactively before handing over documents to avoid needing an extra trip; note 필요하다 takes 사본이 as subject, not object
A: 여권 원본도 가져오셨어요? / B: 네, 사본이랑 원본 둘 다 가져왔어요.
A: Did you bring the original passport too? / B: Yes, I brought both the copy and the original.
A/B exchange: staff confirm both documents; 둘 다 ('both') is the natural way to confirm you have the pair
사본이 없는데 여기서 떼도 돼요?
I don't have a copy — can I make one here?
떼도 돼요 asks if copying on-site is allowed; 없는데 ('I don't have one, but…') frames the problem before the request
nuance: 여권 사본 필요해요? is 여권 ('passport', 旅券) + 사본 ('copy/duplicate', 寫本) + 필요해요 ('is needed'), asking whether a photocopy is required. The crucial pair is 사본 ('a copy') vs 원본 ('the original', 原本): immigration often wants both your passport 원본 (to verify) and a 사본 (to keep on file), so knowing both words prevents a wasted trip. The verb for obtaining an official copy or certificate is 떼다 (literally 'to detach/peel') — 사본 떼다 ('make/get a copy'), 등본 떼다 ('get a certified register extract') — baffling to English speakers because 떼다 usually means 'peel off'; just learn 떼다 = 'obtain an official paper at a counter'. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'copy' as 카피, which Koreans don't use for documents (카피 sounds like advertising copy or computer copy); the document word is 사본. Another trap is the verb 'need': learners say 필요로 해요 (over-literal), but natural Korean is simply 필요해요 ('is needed') — note 필요하다 makes the needed thing the SUBJECT (여권 사본이 필요해요), so 여권 사본을 필요해요 is a particle error. Register plain 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: 여권(passport) + 사본(copy) + 필요해요(is needed). The real function: proactively checking the document checklist before handing anything over, avoiding the common frustration of being told mid-process that you need a copy you don't have. Note: 필요하다 makes the thing needed the SUBJECT — 사본'이' 필요해요, never 사본'을'.

Said at the counter when presenting documents, or before visiting if you're preparing your packet. Register is plain 존댓말. You can confirm you brought both with 사본이랑 원본 둘 다 가져왔어요 ('I brought both copy and original'). Ask about on-site copying with 여기서 사본 뗄 수 있어요? ('can I make a copy here?').

사본 (copy of a document) vs 원본 (the original) — always learn these as a pair. The verb 떼다 ('to obtain an official paper') is the natural action verb: 사본 떼다, 등본 떼다. Saying 사본 만들다 ('make a copy') is understandable but 떼다 is what office Korean sounds like.

여권 사본 필요해요? → 원본도 필요해요? (asking about the original too) → 사본 몇 장 필요해요? (how many copies?). If you need to find the copier: 사본 어디서 떼요? or 복사기 어디 있어요? ('where's the copier?'). Staff may say: 사본 한 장 주세요 ('please give one copy').

두 가지 함정: (1) saying 카피 for a document copy — 카피 sounds like advertising copy; the correct word is 사본. (2) 여권 사본을 필요해요 — 필요하다 takes the subject particle, not object: 여권 사본이 필요해요. The 을/를 particle error is very common.

mistakes: Saying 여권 사본을 필요해요.
필요하다 makes the needed thing the SUBJECT: 여권 사본이 필요해요. Marking it with object 을/를 is ungrammatical.
Using 카피 for a document copy.
카피 reads as 'advertising copy' in Korean. A photocopy/duplicate of a document is 사본: 여권 사본 필요해요?
Not knowing 떼다 for making copies/certificates.
To get an official copy you 떼다 it: 사본 떼다, 등본 떼다. Saying 사본 만들다 is understandable but 떼다 is the natural office verb.

usage: 이 서류 다 준비했어요
I've prepared all these documents
Polite; showing you brought everything
서류 여기 다 있어요
All the documents are here
Simpler 'they're all here' phrasing
서류 이게 다인데 맞아요?
These are all the documents — is that right?
이게 다인데 ('this is everything') asks for confirmation
서류 더 필요한 거 있어요?
Is there any more document I need?
Checking if anything is still missing
examples: 이 서류 다 준비했어요.
I've prepared all these documents.
Set your papers on the counter; the past tense 준비했어요 ('I have prepared') signals completion — staff know to begin checking
A: 서류 다 준비하셨어요? / B: 네, 말씀하신 서류 다 준비했는데 확인해 주세요.
A: Have you prepared all your documents? / B: Yes, I prepared everything you mentioned — please check.
A/B exchange: staff ask with honorific -셨어요; you reply confirming and adding 확인해 주세요 ('please check') to invite verification
서류 다 준비했는데 혹시 빠진 거 있어요?
I prepared everything — is anything possibly missing?
혹시 빠진 거 ('anything possibly left out') invites the clerk to double-check; 혹시 softens the concern and 빠진 거 ('missing thing') is the natural way to ask about gaps
nuance: 이 서류 다 준비했어요 is 이 ('this/these') + 서류 ('documents/paperwork', 書類) + 다 ('all') + 준비하다 ('to prepare', 準備) in past tense, the line that says you've brought everything required. 서류 is the all-purpose word for official papers (forms, certificates, copies) treated as a mass noun — you don't pluralize it, and one paper or a whole stack is still 서류. The verb 준비했어요 (past of 준비하다) is exactly right for 'I have prepared/got ready'. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 of 'documents' as 다큐먼트 or even 문서 in the wrong place: 문서 ('a document/text file') is more about a written document or computer file, while the packet you bring to a government office is 서류 — say 서류 at immigration. Another trap is 다 ('all') placement: 다 goes right before the verb (다 준비했어요), not before the noun as English 'all the documents' might tempt you (it's not 다 서류). The natural softener when handing them over is the -는데 lead-in: 다 준비했는데 확인해 주세요 ('I've prepared everything, so please check'), pairing your statement with a polite request to verify. Register plain 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: Word-for-word: 이 서류(these documents) + 다(all) + 준비했어요(I have prepared). The real function: signaling to the clerk that you believe your document packet is complete so they can begin the intake process — while also opening the door for them to flag anything missing.

Said at the intake window when you place your documents on the counter or slide them through the slot. Register plain 존댓말. The most useful follow-up is 혹시 빠진 거 있어요? ('is anything missing?') — clerks appreciate when applicants actively invite a check rather than assuming everything is correct.

서류 (the official papers you bring to an office — a mass noun) vs 문서 (a written document or computer file). At immigration always say 서류. Also: 이 서류 다 준비했어요 (past, completed action) vs 이 서류 다 있어요 ('all the documents are here', present state) — both work; past 준비했어요 emphasizes your preparation effort.

다 준비했어요 → 다 준비했는데 확인해 주세요 (adds a polite verification request) → 서류 이게 다인데 맞아요? (asks if this is the complete set) → 서류 더 필요한 거 있어요? (checks for gaps). 말씀하신 서류 다 준비했어요 ('I prepared all the documents you mentioned') references the checklist the clerk gave you.

두 가지 함정: (1) 다큐먼트/문서 for the office packet — use 서류. (2) 다 ('all') placement: English places 'all' before the noun ('all the documents'), tempting 다 서류 준비했어요 — but in Korean 다 modifies the verb and goes right before it: 서류 다 준비했어요.

mistakes: Using 문서 for the papers at immigration.
문서 leans toward a written document or file. The packet of official papers is 서류: 이 서류 다 준비했어요.
Placing 다 before the noun: 다 서류 준비했어요.
다 ('all') normally sits right before the verb: 서류 다 준비했어요. Fronting it onto the noun sounds off.
Saying 준비해요 (present) for 'I have prepared'.
Completed preparation is past tense: 준비했어요. 준비해요 sounds like a general/habitual 'I prepare', not 'I've got it ready'.
